concepts.body: Adapt a model from lightest to heaviest. Prompt engineering (system prompt, few-shot examples) shapes format and tone instantly. RAG puts current passages in the prompt at query time, the right answer for facts that change or need citations because a data source sync updates the answers. Fine-tuning is supervised: labeled prompt/response pairs teach a consistent behavior or narrow task, but baked-in knowledge goes stale and cannot be cited. Continued pre-training (where the base model supports it) learns from unlabeled domain text, so it teaches vocabulary such as product codes and jargon. Reinforcement fine-tuning scores outputs with reward functions instead of labeled pairs. Bedrock Model Distillation has a large teacher model answer your prompts (from S3 or invocation logs) and fine-tunes a smaller student, cutting cost and latency while keeping task quality.

concepts.heading: Running Customization Jobs and Serving the Result
concepts.body: Bedrock customization jobs read JSON Lines from S3 in the schema set by job type and base model (prompt and completion, a messages list, or an input text field for continued pre-training), and run as a service role that needs S3 access plus kms:Decrypt on the key for SSE-KMS data. The result is a separate custom model resource: it is invoked through its own on-demand deployment ARN or Provisioned Throughput ARN, never the base model ID, and its weights cannot be downloaded. When full fine-tuning runs out of GPU memory, use LoRA (small trainable adapters on a frozen base) or QLoRA (base also quantized to 4-bit). Custom training code runs in SageMaker AI training jobs; Bedrock Custom Model Import serves the resulting open-weight model serverlessly. Gated JumpStart models need the EULA accepted.

examPoints: When a stem describes labeled tabular data with high volume, low latency and low cost per prediction, the expected answer is a custom supervised model such as XGBoost, not a foundation model.

When knowledge changes often or answers need citations, choose RAG; use fine-tuning for labeled input/output behavior and continued pre-training (where the model supports it) for unlabeled domain text, and distillation when quality is right but cost or latency is not.

When a Bedrock custom model returns base behavior or cannot be called, invoke its deployment or Provisioned Throughput ARN; when a customization job cannot read SSE-KMS data, grant its service role the key permission.

quiz.q: A bank has 3,000 reviewed prompt and response pairs showing the exact tone and JSON layout its assistant must follow. Prompt engineering with many examples still gives inconsistent output, and policy facts are served by a separate knowledge base. What should the ML engineer do next?
choices: Run continued pre-training on the 3,000 pairs, so the model absorbs the vocabulary of the bank from unlabeled text
Fine-tune the model in Bedrock on the labeled pairs, stored as JSON Lines in S3, to lock in tone and layout
Use Model Distillation with a smaller student, because distillation is the technique that fixes inconsistent output layout
Raise the temperature and the maximum token count, so that the model explores more of the output formats it knows
quiz.explain: Labeled input/output pairs teaching a consistent style and format are the case for fine-tuning once prompting has failed. Continued pre-training uses unlabeled text, distillation targets cost and latency, and higher temperature adds randomness rather than consistency.

quiz.q: Ten product teams each need a variant of one open-weight model tuned on their own data. The platform team wants small per-team artifacts and one copy of the large base model on the hosting side. Which approach fits?
choices: Full fine-tuning of the model once per team, each result hosted on its own endpoint to avoid interference between teams
Continued pre-training of the base model on the pooled data of all ten teams, then one shared custom model for everybody
Model Distillation per team into a smaller student, hosted one student per team on separate Provisioned Throughput
LoRA fine-tuning per team, giving a small adapter each, with the adapters served on top of one shared base model
quiz.explain: LoRA freezes the base and trains small adapters, so each team gets a compact artifact and many adapters can share one base model copy. Full fine-tuning and per-team students multiply large artifacts, and pooled continued pre-training gives no team its own variant.

days.recap: Pick a custom model for tabular, high-volume prediction and a prompted FM when labels are missing; choose Bedrock for managed per-token access and JumpStart for control; climb the ladder from prompting to RAG to fine-tuning, continued pre-training and distillation only as needed; and remember that customization jobs use a service role, custom models have their own ARN, and LoRA or QLoRA fits memory limits.

days.title: Evaluating Foundation Models and RAG Applications

concepts.heading: Three Ways to Evaluate in Amazon Bedrock
concepts.body: Bedrock model evaluation offers three modes. Automatic (programmatic) evaluation runs built-in or custom prompt datasets and computes algorithmic metrics such as accuracy, robustness and toxicity: fast and cheap, but limited to what an algorithm can score. Model as a judge (LLM-as-a-judge) has a supported judge model score responses on metrics like correctness, completeness, helpfulness, faithfulness or harmfulness over a JSON Lines prompt dataset in S3; with bring-your-own inference responses it can also judge models that run outside Bedrock. Human-based evaluation lets your own work team rate responses with Likert scales, thumbs up/down or side-by-side comparison of two models, on custom metrics. Expert judgment or required human sign-off means human evaluation.

concepts.heading: Reference-Based Text Metrics
concepts.body: When human-written reference outputs exist, score generated text against them. ROUGE counts overlapping words (ROUGE-1), word pairs (ROUGE-2) or the longest common subsequence (ROUGE-L); it is the classic summarization metric but gives no credit for paraphrase. BLEU is a precision-oriented n-gram overlap metric common for translation. BERTScore compares contextual embeddings token by token, so a paraphrase with the same meaning still scores well. Use ROUGE or BLEU for wording overlap and BERTScore for meaning. Perplexity needs no reference and only reflects how predictable the text is to a language model, and RMSE or AUC-ROC belong to numeric and classification models, so they are distractors for generated text.

concepts.heading: SageMaker Clarify Foundation Model Evaluations
concepts.body: SageMaker Clarify includes foundation model evaluations built on the open-source fmeval library. They run from SageMaker Studio or from code, for example in a pipeline step, against SageMaker AI endpoints, JumpStart models or Bedrock models. The dimensions are accuracy (ROUGE, METEOR, BERTScore, F1, exact match), factual knowledge, prompt stereotyping, semantic robustness (does the output change after typos or extra spaces) and toxicity, with built-in datasets or your own. This is different from Clarify's pre-training and post-training bias metrics and Model Monitor bias drift, which target tabular models. Bedrock Guardrails block harmful content at runtime and are not a pre-release benchmark report.

concepts.heading: Evaluating RAG Systems and Agents
concepts.body: A RAG system retrieves and then generates, so measure both stages. Bedrock RAG evaluations offer retrieve-only jobs, which score retrieval with context relevance (are the passages relevant) and context coverage (do they contain what the reference answer needs), and retrieve-and-generate jobs, which score the full pipeline with correctness, completeness, helpfulness and faithfulness (are the answer's claims supported by the retrieved context). Low context relevance means fixing retrieval through chunking, embeddings, metadata filters or the number of results. High relevance with low faithfulness means fixing generation: prompt instructions, model choice or a guardrail contextual grounding check. Agents need trajectory tests: trace tool calls, order and arguments against a fixed test set, because the final message can look right after a skipped step. Use a judge different from the evaluated model and spot-check it with humans.

examPoints: When a stem requires licensed experts to rate answers on custom criteria or compare two models side by side, the expected answer is Bedrock human-based evaluation with your own work team.

When a stem needs stereotyping, toxicity, robustness or accuracy benchmarks for generated text, the expected answer is SageMaker Clarify foundation model evaluations (fmeval) for SageMaker AI or JumpStart models and pipelines, or Bedrock automatic evaluation for Bedrock models; tabular bias metrics do not apply.
When RAG answers add facts that the relevant retrieved passages do not support, the problem is the generator (low faithfulness); when the retrieved passages are irrelevant, fix retrieval first.

quiz.q: A team measures a RAG assistant. The context coverage score is low: the retrieved passages often lack information that the reference answers need, although the model follows the passages it receives faithfully. Which change targets the problem?
choices: Add a guardrail contextual grounding check so that the model only states claims contained in the passages it received
Switch the judge model to a larger evaluator, because the low coverage score probably comes from an unreliable judge
Lower the temperature of the generator, so that answers stay closer to the wording of the retrieved passages
Improve retrieval: adjust chunking, try a better embedding model, add metadata filters or raise the number of results
quiz.explain: Low context coverage means retrieval misses needed information, so chunking, embeddings, filters and the number of results are the levers. Grounding checks and temperature act on generation, and nothing suggests the judge is faulty.

quiz.q: An engineer scores generated summaries against analyst-written references with ROUGE and finds low scores, yet reviewers say the summaries preserve the meaning with different wording. Which metric best captures what ROUGE misses?
choices: Perplexity, which reflects how predictable the summary is to a language model and uses the reference to compare meaning
RMSE, which measures the numeric distance between the summary text and the reference summary for each document pair
BERTScore, which compares contextual embeddings of both texts, so paraphrases with the same meaning still score well
AUC-ROC, which shows how well the summary ranks the reference text above unrelated texts in the evaluation set
quiz.explain: ROUGE counts overlapping words and gives no credit for paraphrase; BERTScore compares embeddings and rewards meaning. Perplexity uses no reference, and RMSE and AUC-ROC are regression and classification metrics.

days.recap: Choose the evaluation mode by who must judge (algorithm, judge model or your own experts), use ROUGE or BLEU for wording and BERTScore for meaning, run Clarify fmeval for stereotyping, toxicity and robustness before release, and diagnose RAG by stage: low context relevance or coverage means retrieval, low faithfulness means generation.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Model Development and Evaluation

concepts.heading: The Domain 2 Model Development Pipeline
concepts.body: Domain 2 traces a model from initial approach selection through governance: choosing a modeling approach, running and optimizing training jobs including distributed training and Spot training, tuning hyperparameters automatically, evaluating performance with the right metrics for the problem, diagnosing and fixing overfitting or underfitting, and governing model versions and experiment history. At 24% of the exam, Domain 2 is weighted nearly as heavily as Domain 1, and scenario questions frequently combine two of these stages, for example describing an overfitting symptom that arose during a specific HPO configuration.

concepts.heading: Metric Selection Is the Recurring Skill
concepts.body: Across Domain 2, the single most tested skill is correctly matching an evaluation metric to the cost structure of the business problem described: recall when missing positives is costly, precision when false alarms are costly, F1 for balanced concerns, AUC-ROC for threshold-independent comparison, and RMSE versus MAE depending on how heavily large regression errors should be penalized. A large fraction of Domain 2 wrong answers substitute a plausible-sounding but wrong metric, for instance offering accuracy as a distractor whenever the scenario describes an imbalanced dataset.

concepts.heading: Overfitting/Underfitting Diagnosis as a Gateway Skill
concepts.body: Correctly identifying overfitting versus underfitting from a described symptom, a large train/validation gap versus both scores being low, is a gateway skill that then determines which entire category of fix is appropriate: reducing model capacity/variance versus increasing it. Getting this initial diagnosis backwards leads directly to selecting a plausible-sounding but opposite-direction wrong answer, which is one of the more common trap patterns in this domain.

concepts.heading: From Baseline to Governed, Production-Ready Model
concepts.body: Zooming out, Domain 2 traces a model's journey from a first working baseline to something an organization can trust: pick an approach that matches problem standardization and team expertise, train it efficiently using distributed or Spot infrastructure, tune it systematically rather than by guesswork, judge it against a metric that reflects the real business cost of errors, diagnose and correct its generalization behavior, and finally catalog and govern the result so it can be safely promoted. Holding this end-to-end arc in mind turns six days of separate topics into one coherent narrative about turning a rough model into a production-ready asset. Domain 2 in C02 adds generative AI: see the new days "Choosing and customizing foundation models" and "Evaluating foundation models".

examPoints: When a Domain 2 scenario describes a train/validation performance gap, immediately classify it as overfitting first, since that classification determines the entire remaining direction of the answer.

When a Domain 2 scenario mentions cost asymmetry between error types (missing a positive vs. a false alarm), that phrase is almost always pointing at recall vs. precision, respectively, rather than accuracy.
Domain 2 in C02 adds generative AI: see the new days "Choosing and customizing foundation models" and "Evaluating foundation models".

quiz.q: Which condition describes overfitting rather than underfitting?
choices: Both training and validation performance are low
Training performance is high but validation performance is much lower
Training performance is undefined
Overfitting is unrelated to training/validation comparison
quiz.explain: A large gap between high training performance and lower validation performance is the defining signature of overfitting.

quiz.q: In a spam filter, incorrectly flagging a legitimate email as spam (a false positive) is considered more costly than missing a spam email. Which metric should be prioritized?
choices: Recall
Precision
Plain accuracy
RMSE
quiz.explain: Precision measures the proportion of flagged (positive) predictions that are correct, directly addressing the cost of false positives, whereas recall addresses missed positives and RMSE is a regression metric.

days.recap: Domain 2 wraps up as modeling approach selection to training optimization (distributed/Spot) to hyperparameter tuning to metric-driven evaluation to overfitting/underfitting diagnosis to governance (Registry/Experiments), with metric selection and over/underfitting diagnosis as the two most heavily tested skills; C02 adds foundation-model choice, customization and evaluation (new days "Choosing and customizing foundation models" and "Evaluating foundation models").

days.title: Choosing Inference Infrastructure: Real-Time, Serverless, Async, and Batch Endpoints

concepts.heading: Real-Time Inference Endpoints
concepts.body: A real-time SageMaker endpoint runs continuously on provisioned instances and responds to individual prediction requests with low, consistent latency, making it the right choice for interactive applications like a live recommendation widget or a fraud check that must complete within a strict time budget. Because the underlying instances run continuously whether or not requests are arriving, real-time endpoints incur cost around the clock, and capacity must be sized or auto-scaled for peak expected load. This is the default, most flexible inference option and supports features like multi-model endpoints and production variants for A/B testing, discussed later this week.

concepts.heading: Serverless Inference for Intermittent Traffic
concepts.body: Serverless Inference removes the need to provision or manage instances at all: SageMaker automatically provisions compute in response to requests and scales down to zero when there's no traffic, so cost is incurred only when requests actually arrive, ideal for workloads with unpredictable or intermittent traffic where a continuously running endpoint would sit mostly idle. The tradeoff is cold-start latency when a request arrives after a period of inactivity, since compute needs to spin up before it can process the first request. This makes Serverless Inference a poor fit for strict, consistent low-latency requirements but an excellent fit for sporadic internal tools or infrequent API calls.

concepts.heading: Asynchronous Inference for Large or Slow Requests
concepts.body: Asynchronous Inference queues incoming requests and processes them in the background, returning a reference the caller can poll rather than blocking for an immediate response, which suits workloads with large payloads or long processing times where an immediate synchronous response isn't required or even possible within typical API timeout limits. Because requests are queued, Asynchronous Inference can also scale down to zero instances during idle periods like Serverless Inference, combining cost efficiency with support for larger payloads and longer processing times than either real-time or serverless endpoints typically allow. This is the answer whenever a scenario emphasizes large files and no immediate response needed.

concepts.heading: Batch Transform for Offline Bulk Scoring
concepts.body: Batch Transform runs inference across an entire dataset at once as a standalone job, without maintaining any persistent endpoint, making it the most cost-effective option when predictions are needed periodically for large volumes of data rather than continuously for individual requests, for example scoring an entire customer database overnight rather than exposing a live endpoint that mostly sits unused. Because Batch Transform spins up resources only for the duration of the job and shuts them down afterward, it avoids paying for standing endpoint capacity entirely. The choice between Batch Transform and Asynchronous Inference usually comes down to whether the workload is a single, self-contained bulk job or an ongoing stream of individually submitted large/slow requests.

examPoints: A scenario describing highly unpredictable, intermittent traffic where paying for continuously running infrastructure would be wasteful signals Serverless Inference.

A scenario describing large payloads that don't need an immediate response signals Asynchronous Inference, while a single large periodic bulk-scoring job with no need for an endpoint at all signals Batch Transform.

quiz.q: A company's inference traffic is highly unpredictable and often drops to zero for hours at a time, and the company wants to avoid paying for idle infrastructure during those gaps. Which inference option fits best?
choices: A continuously running real-time endpoint sized for peak load
Serverless Inference
Only Batch Transform, run continuously
A large, always-on GPU cluster
quiz.explain: Serverless Inference scales to zero and incurs no cost when there's no traffic, directly matching this unpredictable, intermittent pattern, unlike a continuously running real-time endpoint.

quiz.q: An application needs to process large document uploads where clients don't need an immediate synchronous response. Which inference option is designed for this?
choices: Real-time inference only
Asynchronous Inference
Serverless Inference exclusively
No inference is needed
quiz.explain: Asynchronous Inference queues large or slow requests and processes them in the background, which is exactly suited to large payloads that don't require an immediate response.

days.recap: Real-time endpoints suit continuous low-latency traffic, Serverless Inference suits intermittent traffic without idle cost, Asynchronous Inference suits large payloads without an immediate-response requirement, and Batch Transform suits large, periodic, offline scoring jobs with no persistent endpoint.

days.title: Infrastructure as Code for ML: CloudFormation and CDK

concepts.heading: Codifying SageMaker Resources
concepts.body: SageMaker resources — endpoints, endpoint configurations, notebook instances, training jobs, and more — can be defined declaratively in CloudFormation templates or programmatically in CDK, turning what would otherwise be manual console clicks into version-controlled, reviewable, and repeatable code. This matters because manual console configuration is error-prone and leaves no automatic audit trail of what changed and when, whereas an IaC template lives in source control alongside a pull-request review process like any other code change. Any exam scenario emphasizing reproducible or consistent ML infrastructure across environments is describing this IaC approach rather than manual setup.

concepts.heading: Endpoint Configuration as Code
concepts.body: Defining a SageMaker endpoint configuration in CloudFormation/CDK — instance type and count, auto-scaling policies, and the traffic-weight distribution across multiple production variants — makes every change to that configuration explicit and trackable through normal code review and version control, rather than a silent manual console edit that's hard to attribute or roll back. This is particularly valuable for regulated environments that need to demonstrate exactly when and why an endpoint's configuration changed. Rolling back a bad configuration change also becomes as simple as reverting the template and redeploying, rather than manually reconstructing the previous settings.

concepts.heading: Consistency Across Environments
concepts.body: A single parameterized IaC template can be deployed to development, staging, and production environments with only parameter values differing between them, ensuring the underlying architecture stays consistent and preventing the class of bugs caused by environments silently drifting apart from ad hoc manual configuration. This is especially important for ML infrastructure, where subtle configuration differences, like a different instance type with different available memory, can cause a model that works in staging to behave unexpectedly in production. Exam scenarios about preventing configuration drift between environments point to this parameterized IaC pattern.

concepts.heading: CDK's Programmatic Flexibility
concepts.body: AWS CDK lets infrastructure be expressed in a general-purpose programming language, which makes it straightforward to use loops, conditionals, and functions to define many similar resources, for instance provisioning a set of per-customer endpoints or a family of related pipelines, patterns that would require significant duplication in a static CloudFormation YAML/JSON template. CDK synthesizes down to standard CloudFormation templates under the hood, so it retains all of CloudFormation's deployment guarantees while offering more expressive authoring. For complex, repetitive, or highly parameterized ML infrastructure patterns, CDK's programmability is often preferred over hand-written CloudFormation.

examPoints: A scenario requiring ML infrastructure to be deployed consistently and reproducibly across development, staging, and production environments signals defining that infrastructure as code with CloudFormation or CDK.

A scenario requiring a clear, trackable history of endpoint configuration changes to prevent accidental drift signals managing that configuration through IaC and code review rather than manual console changes.

quiz.q: A company wants its ML infrastructure to be deployed identically and reproducibly across development, staging, and production environments, with a clear change history. What approach should they take?
choices: Manually configure each environment through the console every time
Define the infrastructure as code using CloudFormation or CDK
Let each environment's configuration diverge over time as needed
Document the setup steps only in a wiki page
quiz.explain: IaC via CloudFormation or CDK provides reproducible, version-controlled deployments across environments, unlike manual configuration or documentation alone.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of managing a SageMaker endpoint configuration through Infrastructure as Code rather than manual console changes?
choices: It becomes impossible to track configuration history
It provides change tracking and environment consistency through version control
It always increases cost
It reduces security
quiz.explain: IaC ties configuration changes to version-controlled code review, providing traceability and consistency that manual console changes do not.

days.recap: Codifying SageMaker resources with CloudFormation or CDK turns manual configuration into reproducible, version-controlled infrastructure, with endpoint settings tracked as code, consistency enforced across environments via parameterized templates, and CDK adding programmatic flexibility for repetitive patterns.

days.title: Container-Based ML Deployment: ECS, EKS, and Lambda

concepts.heading: Deploying Custom Inference Containers on ECS/EKS
concepts.body: Instead of a SageMaker endpoint, a team can deploy a custom inference container directly on Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS, which makes sense when the organization already runs its application workloads on one of these container orchestration platforms and wants ML inference operated with the same tooling, deployment pipelines, and observability stack as everything else, or when very fine-grained control over the serving stack is required. This comes at the cost of taking on more operational responsibility that SageMaker would otherwise manage automatically, such as scaling policies and health checks, which must be configured directly in ECS/EKS. The exam frames existing container orchestration investment as the trigger for this pattern over a SageMaker endpoint.

concepts.heading: Lightweight Inference with AWS Lambda
concepts.body: AWS Lambda can host lightweight model inference when the model is small enough to fit within Lambda's container image size limit of 10 GB and call frequency is low or intermittent, giving a fully serverless, pay-per-invocation inference option without managing any servers at all. Cold starts are a real consideration, since a Lambda function that hasn't been invoked recently takes longer to respond to its first request as the runtime initializes, which matters for latency-sensitive use cases but is often acceptable for internal tools or low-traffic endpoints. Lambda-based inference is a strong fit for small models called occasionally, but a poor fit for large models or consistently high, latency-sensitive traffic.

concepts.heading: GPU Node Groups and Autoscaling on EKS
concepts.body: When ML workloads run on EKS, GPU-backed nodes are typically organized into a dedicated node group separate from general-purpose CPU nodes, since GPU instances are more expensive and workload-specific scheduling ensures GPU capacity is reserved for workloads that actually need it. Kubernetes' Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and the Cluster Autoscaler work together to scale the number of inference pods and, in turn, the number of underlying nodes in response to traffic, mirroring the auto-scaling behavior SageMaker endpoints provide natively but requiring explicit Kubernetes-level configuration. This operational overhead is the tradeoff for the flexibility EKS provides.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between SageMaker and Self-Managed Containers
concepts.body: The decision generally comes down to how much a team is already invested in each ecosystem: teams already using SageMaker features like Feature Store, Model Registry, and Model Monitor benefit from SageMaker endpoints' tight integration with that ecosystem, while teams with an established Kubernetes/container platform and operational tooling often prefer EKS/ECS for consistency with how they operate everything else. Choosing self-managed containers means explicitly taking on responsibilities, such as scaling, health checks, and patching the inference container's dependencies, that SageMaker would otherwise absorb. The exam usually signals the answer through which ecosystem is described as already in place at the organization.

examPoints: A scenario describing a company that already runs its microservices on EKS and wants to manage ML inference the same way signals deploying a custom container to EKS rather than defaulting to a SageMaker endpoint.
A scenario describing a small model with low, infrequent call volume and a desire for zero server management signals AWS Lambda-based inference.

quiz.q: A company already runs all of its microservices on Amazon EKS and wants its ML inference workloads managed through the same deployment pipelines and observability tools. What is the most consistent approach?
choices: Insist on a SageMaker endpoint regardless of existing infrastructure
Deploy a custom inference container to the existing EKS cluster
Use Lambda exclusively
Avoid deploying the model at all
quiz.explain: Deploying to the existing EKS cluster keeps ML inference consistent with how the company already operates its other workloads, which a SageMaker endpoint would not natively integrate with as tightly.

quiz.q: A small model is called only a few times per day and the team wants zero server management with pay-per-use billing. What is the most cost-effective option?
choices: A continuously running large EC2 instance
AWS Lambda-based inference
A permanently running EKS GPU cluster
An on-premises server
quiz.explain: Lambda provides serverless, pay-per-invocation execution ideal for infrequent, lightweight inference workloads, unlike continuously running infrastructure options.

days.recap: ECS/EKS deployment fits teams already invested in container orchestration, Lambda suits small, infrequently called models with zero server management, EKS GPU node groups require explicit autoscaling configuration, and the SageMaker-vs-self-managed choice hinges on existing ecosystem investment.

days.title: Multi-Model Endpoints, Multi-Container Endpoints, and Inference Pipelines

concepts.heading: Multi-Model Endpoints for Cost-Efficient Scale
concepts.body: A Multi-Model Endpoint (MME) hosts many models behind a single SageMaker endpoint, dynamically loading a model into memory when it's invoked and evicting less recently used models when memory is needed for others, which dramatically cuts infrastructure cost when there are far too many individual models to justify a dedicated endpoint for each one, the classic example being a per-customer personalized model where any single customer's model is called relatively rarely. The tradeoff is a cold-load latency penalty the first time a specific model is invoked, since it must be loaded from S3 before it can serve a request. MMEs are the go-to answer whenever a scenario describes thousands of individual models with low per-model call volume.

concepts.heading: Multi-Container Endpoints
concepts.body: A multi-container endpoint hosts multiple models built on different frameworks or containers behind one endpoint, invoked either directly, where the caller specifies which container should handle a given request, or serially, where multiple containers process the request one after another in a defined order. This differs from MME, which hosts many instances of a similar model-serving pattern dynamically, by instead supporting a small, fixed set of distinct containers that may use entirely different frameworks or serve entirely different purposes. It's useful for consolidating a handful of heterogeneous models onto shared infrastructure without requiring separate endpoints for each framework.

concepts.heading: Inference Pipelines for Chained Processing
concepts.body: A SageMaker Inference Pipeline chains multiple containers, commonly a preprocessing container, a model-inference container, and a postprocessing container, into a single sequential pipeline exposed as one endpoint, so the same feature transformation logic used at training time can be reused unchanged at inference time, again helping prevent training-serving skew. Callers interact with a single endpoint and receive fully post-processed output, without needing to orchestrate the individual preprocessing/inference/postprocessing steps themselves. This pattern is a natural complement to Feature Store's consistency guarantees, addressing preprocessing-code consistency specifically rather than just feature-value consistency.

concepts.heading: Production Variants and Traffic-Weighted Rollouts
concepts.body: A single SageMaker endpoint can host multiple production variants, different model versions or even entirely different algorithms, simultaneously, each assigned a percentage of incoming traffic via configurable weights, enabling A/B testing or a gradual canary rollout of a new model version without provisioning a completely separate endpoint. This lets a team validate a new model on a small slice of real traffic before committing to a full cutover, catching problems with far less blast radius than an all-at-once deployment. Shifting the weights incrementally toward the new variant, while monitoring its metrics, is the standard safe-rollout pattern the exam associates with production variants.

examPoints: A scenario describing thousands of individual per-customer or per-segment models, each called relatively infrequently, where a dedicated endpoint per model would be too costly, signals a Multi-Model Endpoint.

A scenario describing gradually routing a small percentage of live traffic to a new model version for validation before a full rollout signals weighted traffic splitting across SageMaker production variants.

quiz.q: A company has thousands of individually trained per-customer models, but each model is invoked only a handful of times per day, making a dedicated endpoint for every model prohibitively expensive. What is the most cost-effective serving pattern?
choices: Keep a dedicated endpoint running for every individual model
Host all the models behind a single Multi-Model Endpoint
Merge all customer models into a single generic model
Do not deploy any of the models
quiz.explain: A Multi-Model Endpoint dynamically loads models on demand from a shared endpoint, avoiding the cost of thousands of dedicated, mostly-idle endpoints.

quiz.q: A team wants to route only 5% of live production traffic to a newly trained model version to validate it before a full rollout. What SageMaker feature enables this?
choices: Immediately replacing the old model with 100% traffic
Weighted traffic splitting across production variants
Deploying to a completely separate, unrelated endpoint
Skipping validation entirely
quiz.explain: Production variants let a single endpoint host multiple model versions with configurable traffic weights, supporting exactly this kind of gradual, low-risk validation.

days.recap: Multi-Model Endpoints economically serve many low-traffic models from one endpoint, multi-container endpoints combine a small set of heterogeneous models, inference pipelines chain preprocessing/inference/postprocessing to preserve consistency, and production variants enable weighted A/B or canary rollouts.

days.title: MLOps CI/CD: SageMaker Pipelines and Step Functions

concepts.heading: SageMaker Pipelines for Native ML Orchestration
concepts.body: SageMaker Pipelines orchestrates an entire ML workflow — data preprocessing, training, evaluation, and conditional model registration or deployment — as a directed acyclic graph of steps expressed through the SageMaker Python SDK, with each step's output cached and reusable so re-running a pipeline doesn't redundantly repeat unchanged steps. Because it's purpose-built for SageMaker, it integrates tightly with Model Registry, Experiments, and Feature Store without extra plumbing, and pipeline definitions themselves can be version-controlled like any other code. This tight native integration is what distinguishes Pipelines from a more general-purpose orchestrator for ML-specific workflows.

concepts.heading: AWS Step Functions for General-Purpose Orchestration
concepts.body: AWS Step Functions can also orchestrate SageMaker training and processing jobs, but does so alongside arbitrary combinations of other AWS services — Lambda, ECS tasks, DynamoDB, SNS notifications, and more — through visual state machines with built-in support for complex branching, parallel execution, and retry/error-handling logic. This makes Step Functions the better choice when an ML workflow needs to be tightly interwoven with broader application logic outside the pure ML lifecycle, whereas SageMaker Pipelines is the more natural fit for a workflow that's purely about data-to-model steps. The exam distinguishes the two by whether the described workflow needs services well beyond SageMaker's own ecosystem.

concepts.heading: The Standard MLOps CI/CD Flow
concepts.body: A typical MLOps pipeline chains together: a code commit that triggers a build/test stage, often via AWS CodeBuild as part of CodePipeline, which triggers a SageMaker Pipelines run for training and evaluation, and, only if the evaluation metrics clear a defined bar, registers the resulting model in Model Registry for a human or automated approval step before an automated deployment. This mirrors traditional software CI/CD but adds ML-specific stages that a purely software-focused pipeline wouldn't include. Recognizing this end-to-end shape helps identify which stage a scenario question is actually describing.

concepts.heading: Condition Steps as Automated Quality Gates
concepts.body: A Condition Step in SageMaker Pipelines evaluates a specified metric, for example requiring validation accuracy above 90%, and only allows the pipeline to proceed to the next step, commonly model registration or deployment, if the condition passes, functioning as an automated quality gate that prevents underperforming models from silently reaching production even in a fully automated pipeline. This is the mechanism that lets teams fully automate retraining and redeployment without sacrificing the safety net a human evaluation review would otherwise provide. Any scenario describing automatically blocking deployment when a metric falls short is describing a Condition Step specifically.

examPoints: A scenario requiring end-to-end orchestration of preprocessing, training, evaluation, and conditional deployment natively within the SageMaker ecosystem, with step reuse/caching, signals SageMaker Pipelines.
A scenario requiring automatic blocking of model registration or deployment whenever an evaluation metric falls below a defined threshold signals a Condition Step within the pipeline.

quiz.q: A team wants to orchestrate preprocessing, training, evaluation, and conditional deployment entirely within the SageMaker ecosystem, with automatic caching of unchanged steps. Which service is the most natural fit?
choices: Manually running each step in sequence
SageMaker Pipelines
CloudFormation alone
Lambda alone
quiz.explain: SageMaker Pipelines is purpose-built for native, cacheable, end-to-end ML workflow orchestration within the SageMaker ecosystem.

quiz.q: A pipeline must automatically prevent a model from being registered or deployed whenever its validation accuracy falls below 90%. Which mechanism enforces this?
choices: Always deploying regardless of the metric
A Condition Step in the pipeline
Manual verification for every single run
Skipping evaluation entirely
quiz.explain: A Condition Step gates progression to the next pipeline stage based on whether a specified metric threshold is met, automatically enforcing this quality bar.

days.recap: SageMaker Pipelines natively orchestrates ML-specific workflows with caching, Step Functions orchestrates broader multi-service workflows, the standard MLOps flow chains commit to build to train/evaluate to gated registration to deployment, and Condition Steps act as automated quality gates blocking underperforming models.

days.title: Deploying Foundation Models and Building Agents: Bedrock Inference Options, Knowledge Bases, and AgentCore

concepts.heading: Choosing How to Consume a Model on Amazon Bedrock
concepts.body: Bedrock offers several ways to run the same foundation model, and the scenario's traffic shape picks one. On-demand inference is pay-per-token with no commitment and suits variable interactive traffic, but it shares capacity and can be throttled at peaks. A cross-Region inference profile spreads on-demand requests across several Regions to absorb bursts; a geographic profile (for example US) keeps inference inside that geography when data residency matters, while a global profile does not. Provisioned Throughput dedicates capacity, sized in model units and bought for a term, for steady forecastable traffic that needs guaranteed throughput. Batch inference takes JSONL records from S3, writes results to S3 and costs less per token, so it fits large offline jobs with a deadline instead of a latency target.

concepts.heading: Hosting Open-Weight Models on SageMaker AI
concepts.body: When the model is not served by Bedrock, SageMaker AI hosts it on an endpoint. A large model that does not fit in one GPU is served from a Large Model Inference (LMI) container that shards the weights with tensor parallelism; the parallel degree normally equals the number of GPUs on the instance, so 140 GB of 16-bit weights fit across eight 40 GB GPUs. Inference components let several models, even with different containers, share one endpoint: each component reserves its own accelerators and memory and scales its own copy count. For chat experiences, streaming returns tokens as they are generated: ConverseStream or InvokeModelWithResponseStream on Bedrock, InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream on a SageMaker AI endpoint.

concepts.heading: Scaling LLM Endpoints, Including to Zero
concepts.body: Asynchronous inference queues large or slow requests, such as 200 MB document bundles that run for minutes, and its auto scaling minimum can be zero so an idle endpoint costs nothing. The classic trap is scaling out from zero: a target-tracking policy on backlog per instance has nothing to divide by when no instance runs, so queued requests wait forever. The fix is an additional step scaling policy driven by the HasBacklogWithoutCapacity metric, which starts the first instance; target tracking then handles further scale-out. Real-time endpoints keep at least one instance and trade idle cost for low, steady latency.

concepts.heading: Knowledge Bases: Creating One Does Not Load It
concepts.body: A Bedrock knowledge base turns documents in a data source such as S3 into chunks, embeds them and stores the vectors in a vector store, and the Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate APIs query it. Deploying the knowledge base and data source with CloudFormation or CDK creates only configuration: nothing is searchable until an ingestion job runs (StartIngestionJob), and again after every content change. Ingestion is asynchronous, so a pipeline must wait for it to complete before testing retrieval. Because Kendra is closed to new customers, Knowledge Bases is the managed retrieval choice for new RAG applications.

concepts.heading: Agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
concepts.body: Amazon Bedrock Agents was renamed Agents Classic and is closed to new customers, so new agent work uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a set of modular services. AgentCore Runtime is serverless hosting for agents written with any framework (LangGraph, for example) or model, running each user session isolated from other sessions and supporting long multi-step tasks. AgentCore Gateway converts existing REST APIs and Lambda functions into tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) behind one endpoint, so you do not write an MCP server per API. AgentCore Memory lets an agent remember user preferences across separate conversations. Observability for agents is covered on the monitoring day.

examPoints: Large non-interactive Bedrock workloads with a deadline but no latency target signal batch inference; steady, forecastable traffic needing guaranteed throughput signals Provisioned Throughput; throttling at peaks with a residency rule signals the matching geographic cross-Region inference profile.

Several open-weight models with different containers on one GPU endpoint, each scaling independently, signal SageMaker AI inference components; a model bigger than one GPU signals an LMI container with tensor parallelism.

Retrieve returning nothing after a successful stack deployment signals a missing ingestion job; a new framework-based agent needing serverless, session-isolated hosting signals AgentCore Runtime, and existing APIs as MCP tools signal AgentCore Gateway.

quiz.q: A lender must classify about 3 million archived loan documents with a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. Results are needed within two days, no user waits on any single response, and the team wants the lowest cost per token without managing a client fleet. Which option fits best?
choices: Bedrock on-demand InvokeModel calls from an auto-scaled fleet of Lambda functions with retries
Bedrock batch inference reading JSONL records from S3 and writing results back to S3
Provisioned Throughput purchased for a one-year term and sized for the nightly peak load
A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with the model deployed on a large multi-GPU instance
quiz.explain: Batch inference is built for large offline workloads with a deadline instead of a latency target, runs at a lower price than on-demand and avoids per-request throttling. Provisioned Throughput and a real-time endpoint bill for standing capacity that sits idle most of the day.

quiz.q: An asynchronous inference endpoint hosts an open-weight LLM. To keep idle-night cost at zero, auto scaling allows a minimum of 0 instances and uses target tracking on backlog per instance. After an idle night, new requests stay queued and no instance starts. What should the ML engineer add while keeping scale to zero?
choices: A higher target value on the existing backlog-per-instance target-tracking policy, so scale-out triggers later
A minimum capacity of 1 instance, which removes the zero-instance state but also the idle-night savings
A step scaling policy and alarm on the HasBacklogWithoutCapacity metric to start the first instance
A longer invocation timeout on the endpoint so queued requests stop expiring while they wait for capacity
quiz.explain: With no running instance, backlog per instance cannot trigger scale-out. A step scaling policy on HasBacklogWithoutCapacity starts the first instance, and target tracking then takes over, so the endpoint can still return to zero when idle.

days.recap: Pick the Bedrock option by traffic shape: on-demand for variable load, cross-Region profiles for peaks, Provisioned Throughput for guaranteed steady load, batch for offline jobs. Open-weight models use SageMaker AI with LMI tensor parallelism and inference components. Knowledge bases need an ingestion job, and new agents go on AgentCore (Runtime, Gateway, Memory).

days.title: CI/CD and Orchestration for Foundation Model Workflows: Versioning, Evaluation Gates, and IaC

concepts.heading: Version Everything That Changes Model Behavior
concepts.body: A generative AI release is more than code: the prompt text, the guardrail, the flow and the model choice all change behavior. Bedrock Prompt Management keeps a working draft you edit freely and lets you create numbered, immutable prompt versions; production calls the versioned prompt, never the draft, so each release is traceable to an exact prompt text. Guardrails work the same way: a draft guardrail changes live traffic the moment it is edited, while a published numeric version is stable until the pin is moved. Bedrock Flows add aliases on top: the application always calls the prod alias, and promotion or rollback is one alias update between immutable flow versions with no code change.

concepts.heading: Infrastructure as Code for GenAI Stacks
concepts.body: Guardrails, knowledge bases, data sources and Lambda functions can be declared in CloudFormation or the AWS CDK, reviewed in Git and deployed the same way in every environment. Defining the guardrail as code and publishing a version per release means production changes only when a release deploys, not when someone tunes a filter in the console. Rules can be enforced before deployment: CDK assertions unit tests synthesize the template in the pull-request build and fail it when, for example, a guardrail lacks a sensitive-information (PII) filter. A knowledge base resource creates configuration only, so the pipeline needs a step that runs the ingestion job after deployment.

concepts.heading: Orchestrating Long-Running Jobs with Step Functions and SageMaker Pipelines
concepts.body: Bedrock model customization can run for hours. A Step Functions state machine uses the optimized .sync integration so the state waits for the job to finish, however long that takes, then continues to evaluation and notification, with failures routed to a Catch, and no custom polling code. The same pattern refreshes a knowledge base nightly: start the ingestion job, wait for completion, run a retrieval quality check, alert on failure, all triggered on a schedule. For open-weight fine-tuning on SageMaker AI, SageMaker Pipelines trains, evaluates and registers passing models in the Model Registry with a status such as PendingManualApproval; an EventBridge rule on the Model Package State Change event, filtered to Approved for that model package group, starts deployment without polling.

concepts.heading: Evaluation Gates and Promoting One Artifact
concepts.body: Passing unit tests does not show that answers stay good, so a GenAI pipeline adds behavioral gates before production: a Bedrock evaluation job scores the candidate prompt and model on a golden set and fails the stage below a threshold, and ApplyGuardrail red-team tests check safety regressions. Both gates fail the build automatically, like the Condition Step in a SageMaker pipeline. Artifacts follow the build-once rule: build the agent container image once, push it to Amazon ECR and deploy the same immutable image digest to staging and production, because rebuilding per stage lets a dependency change between the tested build and the shipped one.

examPoints: Production that must change only on release, with traceability, signals a Bedrock prompt version or guardrail version referenced by number (never DRAFT), and a flow alias moved between versions for promotion and rollback.

Waiting for a many-hour Bedrock job without custom polling signals Step Functions with the .sync integration; starting deployment when a reviewer approves a model signals an EventBridge rule on the SageMaker Model Package State Change event.

Blocking promotion when answer quality or safety regresses signals an evaluation-job gate on a golden set plus guardrail red-team tests; a tested image that differs from the shipped one signals build once and promote the same ECR digest.

quiz.q: Developers keep editing a Bedrock guardrail in the console while production calls it, and one filter tweak changed live behavior immediately. The team wants changes reviewed in Git and production to change only when a release deploys. What should they do?
choices: Define the guardrail in CloudFormation or CDK, publish a numbered version per release and pin production to that version
Restrict console edits to senior engineers and keep production pointed at the guardrail working draft after review
Copy the guardrail into a second account each week and point production at the copy for the next release
Move the filter rules into application code and call the model without any guardrail attached to the request
quiz.explain: A draft changes live traffic as soon as it is edited. A guardrail managed as code publishes an immutable version per release, and production pinned to that version is unaffected by later draft edits until the pin is changed by a deployment.

quiz.q: A CodePipeline pipeline promotes a new Bedrock prompt version and agent image from staging to production. The team wants promotion blocked automatically when answer quality regresses, and the same tested image to reach production. Which design meets both needs?
choices: Rebuild the image in the production stage and have an engineer read a sample of answers before promoting it
An evaluation job on a golden set that fails below a threshold, and one ECR image digest deployed to both stages
Deploy to production first and watch CloudWatch error metrics for a week before deciding whether to roll back
Deploy the prompt draft to production and rely on guardrail filters to catch any weak answers after release
quiz.explain: An evaluation job on a golden set gates quality automatically, and promoting one immutable digest guarantees production runs exactly what was tested. Rebuilding per stage, manual spot checks or production-first rollouts all leave a gap the pipeline should close.

days.recap: Treat prompts, guardrails and flows as versioned artifacts: numbered versions and aliases give traceable releases and quick rollback. Declare GenAI stacks as code and unit-test the synthesized template. Orchestrate long jobs with Step Functions .sync or SageMaker Pipelines plus EventBridge approval, gate releases on evaluation jobs, and promote one built image digest.

days.title: Domain 3 Review: Deployment and Orchestration

concepts.heading: The Domain 3 Deployment Decision Chain
concepts.body: Domain 3 moves from choosing inference infrastructure matched to traffic pattern (real-time, serverless, async, batch), through codifying that infrastructure reproducibly with IaC, to container-based alternatives when existing platform investment favors them, to more advanced serving patterns like multi-model endpoints and traffic-weighted rollouts, and finally to automating the whole training-to-deployment workflow with SageMaker Pipelines. At 24% weight, it matches Domains 2 and 4 and still requires fluency across this full chain, since scenario questions often combine an inference-type decision with a deployment-automation detail in the same question.

concepts.heading: Traffic Pattern Recognition Drives Endpoint Choice
concepts.body: The fastest way to answer a Domain 3 endpoint-selection question is to extract three facts from the scenario: whether traffic is predictable or bursty, what latency requirement is stated, and how many distinct models need to be served. Predictable, latency-sensitive traffic with a manageable number of models points to real-time endpoints; unpredictable/intermittent traffic points to Serverless Inference; large payloads without an immediate-response need point to Asynchronous Inference; a single big offline job points to Batch Transform; and very large numbers of low-traffic models point to Multi-Model Endpoints regardless of which base inference type is otherwise implied.

concepts.heading: Automation and Governance as the Domain's Throughline
concepts.body: Nearly every topic in this domain — IaC, condition steps, production variants — exists to make deployment safer and more repeatable rather than faster in isolation: IaC prevents configuration drift, condition steps prevent bad models from being promoted, and weighted production variants prevent risky all-at-once cutovers. Recognizing that Domain 3 questions are frequently really testing which mechanism reduces risk in this deployment scenario, rather than purely which service is fastest, helps eliminate distractor answers that optimize for speed at the expense of safety.

concepts.heading: From a Trained Model to a Living Production System
concepts.body: Zooming out, Domain 3 answers how a model that exists only as an artifact in Model Registry becomes something users or downstream systems can actually call: pick infrastructure matched to how the model will really be used, express that infrastructure as reviewable code, decide whether to lean on SageMaker's managed serving or an existing container platform, layer in patterns that let many models or versions share infrastructure safely, and wrap the whole path from trained model to live traffic in an automated, gated pipeline. This arc is the bridge between Domain 2's model development and Domain 4's ongoing operation. Domain 3 in C02 adds generative AI: see the new days "Deploying FMs and building agents" and "CI/CD and orchestration for FM workflows".

examPoints: When a Domain 3 scenario is ambiguous between two inference types, re-extract traffic predictability, latency requirement, and model count from the scenario text before choosing.

A Domain 3 distractor answer that proposes an immediate, unvalidated full cutover to a new model version is usually wrong whenever the scenario emphasizes safety or gradual validation — production variants or a Condition Step are the safer, correct pattern.
Domain 3 in C02 adds generative AI: see the new days "Deploying FMs and building agents" and "CI/CD and orchestration for FM workflows".

quiz.q: Which inference option is most appropriate for highly unpredictable traffic where the team wants to avoid paying for continuously running, idle infrastructure?
choices: A continuously running real-time endpoint
Serverless Inference
Batch Transform only
A permanently running EKS GPU cluster
quiz.explain: Serverless Inference scales to zero during idle periods, avoiding the cost of continuously running infrastructure for unpredictable traffic.

quiz.q: Which SageMaker Pipelines feature automatically prevents deployment when an evaluation metric fails to meet a defined threshold?
choices: Condition Step
Multi-Model Endpoint
Production Variant
Feature Store
quiz.explain: The Condition Step gates pipeline progression based on whether a metric threshold is met, directly blocking deployment of underperforming models.

days.recap: Domain 3 wraps up as: choose deployment infrastructure by traffic pattern, codify it reproducibly, consider container platforms when already in use, layer in multi-model/traffic-splitting patterns for scale and safety, and automate the whole pipeline with quality gates; C02 adds FM deployment, agents and FM CI/CD (new days "Deploying FMs and building agents" and "CI/CD and orchestration for FM workflows").

days.title: Monitoring Models in Production with SageMaker Model Monitor

concepts.heading: Continuous Baseline Comparison
concepts.body: SageMaker Model Monitor continuously compares the actual data flowing into a production endpoint against a statistical baseline computed from the training dataset, automatically flagging when live traffic's distribution has drifted meaningfully away from what the model was trained on. This baseline-versus-live comparison runs on a schedule without requiring a human to manually pull and compare samples, surfacing drift issues long before they might otherwise be noticed through a slow, hard-to-diagnose decline in business metrics. Model Monitor integrates with SageMaker endpoints by capturing a sample of inference requests and responses for this ongoing analysis.

concepts.heading: Data Quality Monitoring
concepts.body: Data Quality Monitoring specifically watches for shifts in the distribution of input features compared to the training baseline, for example a retailer's customer-behavior features shifting meaningfully during a holiday season compared to the data the model was originally trained on. Detecting this kind of input drift early is valuable because a model's assumptions about normal input ranges, learned entirely from historical training data, can silently become invalid as the real world changes, well before the model's actual prediction quality is confirmed to have degraded. This monitor type doesn't require ground-truth labels, which makes it useful for continuous, low-friction monitoring even when true outcomes aren't yet known.

concepts.heading: Model Quality Monitoring
concepts.body: Model Quality Monitoring compares the model's predictions against ground-truth labels once those actual outcomes become available, tracking metrics like accuracy or F1-score over time to detect genuine performance degradation rather than just input drift. Because ground truth often arrives with a delay, this monitor type necessarily lags Data Quality Monitoring, but it answers the more directly actionable question of has the model actually gotten worse, which is the key trigger for deciding when retraining is truly warranted. Both monitor types are frequently used together, since input drift alone doesn't guarantee performance has degraded.

concepts.heading: Bias Drift and Feature Attribution Drift
concepts.body: Model Monitor also integrates with Clarify to track bias drift, whether fairness metrics that were acceptable at training time shift unfavorably over time in production, and feature attribution drift, whether the relative importance of different features in driving predictions changes meaningfully from what was observed during training. These specialized monitors extend the is anything drifting question beyond raw input distributions and prediction accuracy into fairness and interpretability concerns that matter especially in regulated industries. A scenario asking whether a model's fairness properties are holding up over time in production is describing bias drift monitoring specifically.

examPoints: A scenario about automatically detecting whether the live input data reaching a production endpoint has drifted from the training-time distribution signals Model Monitor's Data Quality Monitoring.

A scenario about determining whether actual model performance has degraded over time, once ground-truth outcomes become available, in order to decide when to retrain, signals Model Quality Monitoring.

quiz.q: A team wants to automatically detect whether the distribution of incoming production data has shifted away from the training data distribution, without needing ground-truth labels. Which capability fits?
choices: Model Quality Monitoring
Data Quality Monitoring
AWS CloudTrail
SageMaker Ground Truth
quiz.explain: Data Quality Monitoring compares live input feature distributions to the training baseline and does not require ground-truth labels, unlike Model Quality Monitoring.

quiz.q: A team wants to determine whether a deployed model's actual predictive accuracy has degraded over time, once true outcomes become available, in order to decide when retraining is needed. Which capability fits?
choices: Data Quality Monitoring only
Model Quality Monitoring, comparing predictions against ground truth
Ignoring monitoring entirely
Only checking input data volume
quiz.explain: Model Quality Monitoring specifically compares predictions to actual ground-truth outcomes to track genuine performance degradation over time.

days.recap: Model Monitor continuously compares live production data against a training baseline, Data Quality Monitoring flags input drift without needing ground truth, Model Quality Monitoring flags real performance degradation once ground truth arrives, and bias/feature-attribution drift extend this to fairness and interpretability.

days.title: Monitoring Infrastructure and Optimizing Cost

concepts.heading: CloudWatch Metrics for SageMaker Endpoints
concepts.body: Amazon CloudWatch automatically collects operational metrics for SageMaker endpoints — invocation count, model latency, error rates, and instance-level CPU/GPU/memory utilization — giving teams visibility into whether an endpoint is over- or under-provisioned relative to actual demand. Consistently low CPU/GPU utilization alongside steady invocation traffic suggests over-provisioning, an opportunity to downsize instance type or count, while high latency or elevated error rates during traffic spikes suggest under-provisioning. These metrics also feed CloudWatch Alarms, which can trigger notifications or automated remediation when thresholds are breached.

concepts.heading: Endpoint Auto-Scaling
concepts.body: SageMaker endpoint auto-scaling automatically adjusts the number of instances behind an endpoint based on a target tracking metric, most commonly invocations-per-instance or model latency, scaling out during traffic surges to maintain responsiveness and scaling back in during quiet periods to avoid paying for idle capacity. This directly addresses the tension between over-provisioning for peak load, wasting money most of the time, and under-provisioning for average load, causing latency spikes during bursts. Auto-scaling configuration includes minimum and maximum instance counts and a cooldown period to prevent rapid oscillation in response to short-lived traffic spikes.

concepts.heading: Cost Explorer for Attributing ML Spend
concepts.body: AWS Cost Explorer, combined with a consistent resource-tagging strategy, tagging SageMaker jobs and endpoints by project, team, or model, lets an organization break down and attribute ML spend to specific initiatives, answering questions like which project is consuming the most training compute this quarter that would otherwise require manually parsing a consolidated bill. This tag-based cost attribution is essential once an organization runs enough concurrent ML projects that a single aggregate bill no longer provides actionable insight into where cost is actually going. Cost Explorer's forecasting and anomaly-detection features can also flag unexpected spend spikes early.

concepts.heading: Cost Optimization Strategies
concepts.body: Beyond right-sizing via CloudWatch metrics and AWS Compute Optimizer's automated instance-type recommendations, common ML cost-optimization tactics include using Managed Spot Training for development and experimentation workloads that can tolerate interruption, and preferring Serverless Inference or Multi-Model Endpoints over continuously running dedicated endpoints for lower-traffic or many-model production scenarios. These tactics target different phases of the ML lifecycle, training-time cost control versus inference-time cost control, and are typically applied together as a holistic cost strategy rather than any single tactic in isolation. Compute Optimizer's recommendations are based on actual historical utilization data rather than guesswork.

examPoints: A scenario asking whether a production inference endpoint's instances are over-provisioned relative to actual traffic signals checking CloudWatch utilization metrics and AWS Compute Optimizer recommendations.
A scenario asking which team or project is responsible for the largest share of ML-related AWS spend signals tag-based analysis in AWS Cost Explorer.

quiz.q: A team suspects its SageMaker inference endpoint instances are much larger than actual traffic requires, wasting money. What is the best way to confirm this?
choices: Guess based on intuition alone
Review CloudWatch utilization metrics and AWS Compute Optimizer recommendations
Always provision the largest instance type available
Ignore the issue since cost doesn't matter
quiz.explain: CloudWatch metrics and Compute Optimizer recommendations are based on actual observed utilization, giving a data-driven basis for right-sizing rather than guesswork.

quiz.q: A company runs several ML projects and wants to determine which specific project is responsible for the largest share of AWS costs. What is the best approach?
choices: Review only the total consolidated bill
Tag resources by project and analyze costs with AWS Cost Explorer
Avoid tracking costs by project
Manually estimate costs without tooling
quiz.explain: Tag-based analysis in Cost Explorer breaks down spend by project or team, which a consolidated bill alone cannot provide.

days.recap: CloudWatch exposes endpoint latency, invocation, and utilization metrics that reveal over- or under-provisioning, auto-scaling adjusts capacity to traffic automatically, Cost Explorer attributes spend by tag across projects, and cost optimization combines right-sizing, Spot training, and serverless/multi-model serving.

days.title: Securing ML Resources: IAM, VPC, and KMS

concepts.heading: Least-Privilege IAM Execution Roles
concepts.body: Every SageMaker notebook instance, training job, and endpoint runs under an IAM execution role that should be scoped to only the specific S3 buckets, KMS keys, and other AWS resources that job actually needs, following the principle of least privilege rather than granting broad access as a matter of convenience. Overly permissive execution roles are a common security finding, since a compromised or misconfigured training job with excessive permissions could read or modify far more data than the job legitimately requires. Separate, narrowly scoped roles per project or pipeline stage limit the blast radius of any single credential being misused.

concepts.heading: VPC Attachment and Network Isolation
concepts.body: Attaching SageMaker training jobs, processing jobs, and notebook instances to a VPC ensures that traffic to and from those resources stays within a private network rather than traversing the public internet, which is frequently a compliance requirement in regulated industries handling sensitive data. The separate Network Isolation option goes further by completely blocking any outbound network access from the training/processing container, preventing any possibility of data exfiltration through an unexpected network call, at the cost of also blocking legitimate outbound calls the job might otherwise need. Both settings are configured per job, not globally.

concepts.heading: Encryption with AWS KMS
concepts.body: AWS KMS provides the encryption keys used to protect ML data at rest across the pipeline: training data and model artifacts stored in S3, and the EBS volumes attached to SageMaker notebook instances and training instances, can all be encrypted using either AWS-managed or customer-managed KMS keys. Customer-managed keys additionally give the security team direct control over key rotation policies and the ability to revoke access by disabling a key, which AWS-managed keys don't offer to the same degree. A scenario requiring encryption of sensitive training data and model artifacts at rest, especially with specific key-management or auditability requirements, points to customer-managed KMS keys.

concepts.heading: Combining These Controls for Regulated Workloads
concepts.body: Regulated workloads typically require all three controls together — least-privilege IAM roles, VPC attachment with network isolation, and KMS encryption at rest — rather than any single control in isolation, since each addresses a distinct threat: IAM limits who or what can access resources, VPC/network isolation limits where traffic can travel, and KMS protects data even if storage media were somehow accessed directly. Exam scenarios describing regulated or highly sensitive ML workloads often expect recognition that multiple layered controls, not one silver-bullet service, are the correct answer.

examPoints: A scenario requiring that ML training run entirely within a private network, isolated from the internet, due to a regulatory requirement signals VPC attachment combined with Network Isolation.

A scenario requiring that sensitive training data and model artifacts be encrypted at rest, especially with specific key-rotation or access-revocation control, signals AWS KMS with customer-managed keys.

quiz.q: A financial services company must ensure its SageMaker training jobs handling sensitive customer data never have any outbound network access, to eliminate any possibility of data exfiltration. Which setting enforces this?
choices: Running in a public subnet with no restrictions
Enabling Network Isolation on the training job
Using the broadest possible IAM role
Disabling encryption for faster training
quiz.explain: Network Isolation completely blocks outbound network access from the training container, directly eliminating exfiltration risk through the network.

quiz.q: Which AWS service manages the encryption keys used to protect S3-stored training data and model artifacts, as well as EBS volumes attached to SageMaker instances, at rest?
choices: AWS WAF
AWS KMS
Amazon Cognito
AWS Shield
quiz.explain: KMS manages the encryption keys used for S3 and EBS encryption at rest; WAF, Cognito, and Shield address different security concerns.

days.recap: Least-privilege IAM execution roles limit resource access, VPC attachment with Network Isolation keeps sensitive training traffic private, KMS encrypts data at rest across S3 and EBS, and regulated workloads typically require all three controls layered together.

days.title: Model Governance and Automated Retraining Pipelines

concepts.heading: Model Cards for Governance Documentation
concepts.body: A Model Card documents a model's intended purpose, the training data used, measured performance, known limitations, and the scope of appropriate use, creating a standardized, human-readable record that supports transparency and accountability when a model is reviewed internally or by an external auditor. This documentation matters especially as an organization accumulates many models over time, since institutional knowledge about why a specific model was built and what its limitations are can otherwise be lost when the original team moves on. SageMaker Model Cards can be generated with information automatically pulled from training jobs and evaluation results, reducing the manual documentation burden.

concepts.heading: Automated Retraining Triggers
concepts.body: When SageMaker Model Monitor detects meaningful data or model drift, it can emit an event that Amazon EventBridge captures and routes to automatically trigger a SageMaker Pipelines retraining workflow, closing the loop between drift detected and retraining started without requiring a human to notice the alert and manually kick off retraining. This automation is valuable because drift can occur gradually or at inconvenient times, and a fully automated response ensures a degrading model doesn't continue serving unchecked for an extended, unmonitored period. The retraining pipeline itself still typically includes the same evaluation and approval gates as any other model promotion.

concepts.heading: Maintaining Approval Gates Even When Automated
concepts.body: Even when retraining is triggered automatically, the resulting model should go through the same evaluation, Model Registry registration, approval, and deployment governance sequence as any manually initiated model, rather than skipping approval on the assumption that automation implies correctness. This preserves a human or automated quality checkpoint specifically at the promotion boundary, preventing a scenario where a retraining pipeline that itself has a bug automatically promotes a worse model to production unchecked. The exam treats automated but still governed as the correct pattern over automated and ungoverned.

concepts.heading: Champion/Challenger Safe Rollout
concepts.body: Rather than immediately replacing the current production model, the champion, with a freshly retrained model, the challenger, at full traffic, the champion/challenger pattern routes a small portion of live traffic to the challenger first, monitors its real-world performance against the champion, and only shifts to full traffic once the challenger has proven itself safe, using the same production-variant traffic-weighting mechanism used for standard A/B testing. This pattern specifically protects against retraining pipelines that pass automated evaluation metrics but still behave unexpectedly on live traffic in ways offline evaluation didn't catch. A scenario emphasizing safe validation before a full switch to a newly retrained model describes this pattern.

examPoints: A scenario requiring that data drift automatically trigger a retraining pipeline without human intervention signals Model Monitor combined with EventBridge and SageMaker Pipelines.

A scenario requiring that a freshly retrained model be validated safely on a portion of live traffic before fully replacing the current production model signals the champion/challenger pattern via weighted production variants.

quiz.q: A company wants data drift detected by Model Monitor to automatically kick off a retraining pipeline without waiting for a person to notice and act. Which combination achieves this?
choices: Manual retraining only, triggered by periodic human review
Model Monitor drift events routed through EventBridge to trigger SageMaker Pipelines
Ignoring drift alerts
Deleting the training data
quiz.explain: EventBridge captures Model Monitor's drift events and can automatically trigger a SageMaker Pipelines retraining run, closing the loop without manual intervention.

quiz.q: After automated retraining produces a new model, the team wants to validate it safely on live traffic before fully replacing the current production model. What pattern should they use?
choices: Immediately switch 100% of traffic to the new model
Use a champion/challenger pattern, routing a small portion of traffic to the new model first
Run the old and new models with no traffic routed to either
Skip retraining validation entirely
quiz.explain: The champion/challenger pattern validates a new model on a limited slice of live traffic before a full cutover, reducing the risk of an unvalidated full replacement.

days.recap: Model Cards document governance details for transparency, automated retraining chains Model Monitor drift detection through EventBridge into SageMaker Pipelines, retrained models still pass through the same approval gates, and the champion/challenger pattern validates new models safely before a full rollout.

days.title: Logging and Audit: CloudTrail and SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking

concepts.heading: CloudTrail for API-Level Audit
concepts.body: AWS CloudTrail records every API call made against SageMaker and other AWS services — who made the call, when, from where, and what the call did, such as creating or deleting a training job or endpoint — providing the audit trail regulated industries need to demonstrate accountability for infrastructure changes. Because CloudTrail logging is largely automatic once enabled and centralizes records across accounts and regions, it's the default answer whenever a scenario asks who did what, and when regarding AWS resource changes rather than about the ML data or model itself. CloudTrail logs can also feed automated alerting when specific sensitive API calls occur.

concepts.heading: ML Lineage Tracking for Data-to-Model Traceability
